label: Losing a Spouse
framing: To lose a spouse is to lose the one you became one flesh with, and the tearing is felt in the body, the bed, the empty chair, the thousand small habits built around a person no longer there. Scripture gives the widow and widower a particular tenderness, naming them again and again as those God himself draws near to defend and provide for.
cultural: Our culture often grants the grieving spouse a brief window of sympathy and then expects them to move on, leaving them to face the long, slow loneliness mostly alone. The Bible places the care of widows near the heart of true religion, charging the community to see them, provide for them, and not abandon them to grief, because the God of Scripture is, by his own name, the defender of those who have lost their partner.
historical: Naomi, in the time of the judges, was so undone by widowhood that she asked to be called Bitter, and yet was carried by the steadfast love of those around her. The early church organized real care for its widows from its first days, and across the centuries the church has counted the comfort of the bereaved spouse, and the guarding of their loneliness, as a frontline duty of the people of God.
application: Do not rush the grief or let others rush you, for this loss reshapes a whole life and takes far longer than the world allows. Let the church surround you, especially in the lonely evenings and weekends when the absence is loudest, and accept the meals, the company, the help with what your spouse used to carry. Lean on your pastor and a grief counselor or a widows and widowers group, and pray the laments, holding to the promise that you do not grieve as those without hope.

verses.text: She died in Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went out to mourn and to weep for her.
verses.where: Sarah dies at Hebron, and Abraham comes to mourn and weep for her. The chapter goes on to legal business, the purchase of a grave, but it begins with grief. The man held up through Scripture as the father of faith wept for his wife, and then got up and did the hard practical things a death requires.

verses.text: Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm. For love is as strong as death, its jealousy as unrelenting as Sheol. Its sparks are fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all.
verses.where: The Song's great statement about love: set me as a seal over your heart, for love is as strong as death, and many waters cannot quench it. A seal was worn on the body and marked what belonged to someone. Scripture does not set married love against death as the weaker thing. It names them as equals in strength.

verses.text: But Ruth replied: “Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you. For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.
verses.where: Three women in Moab have buried their husbands. Naomi tells her widowed daughters-in-law to go home, and Ruth refuses: where you go I will go, and only death will part us. The book that begins with three widows goes on to show God's kindness reaching them through a loyalty no one could have expected.

verses.text: Then Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, “May he be blessed by the LORD, who has not withdrawn His kindness from the living or the dead.” Naomi continued, “The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers.”
verses.where: Naomi, who had told the town to call her bitter, hears whose field Ruth gleaned in that day and blesses the LORD, who has not withdrawn his kindness from the living or the dead. The first small sign of provision lets her say that God's kindness still reaches her husband and sons who died, and the two women left behind.

verses.text: A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation. God settles the lonely in families; He leads the prisoners out to prosperity, but the rebellious dwell in a sun-scorched land.
verses.where: In the middle of a psalm of God's triumphant march, David names who this mighty God is for: a father of the fatherless and a defender of the widows. In a world where a widow had no one to speak for her in court or protect her land, God himself takes that place. And he settles the lonely in families.

verses.text: He executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing.
verses.where: Moses describes the God of gods, great and awesome, who cannot be bribed, and then says what he does with that power: he executes justice for the fatherless and the widow. The widow is named among the three people most at risk in Israel's world, and God's law protects her by name.

verses.text: There was also a prophetess named Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, who was well along in years. She had been married for seven years, and then was a widow to the age of eighty-four. She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying.
verses.where: Anna was married seven years and then lived as a widow into great old age, worshiping in the temple night and day. When the infant Jesus is brought in, she gives thanks and speaks about him to everyone waiting. A life many would have called empty is the one Luke gives the last word in the temple scene.

verses.text: The widow who is truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God and continues night and day in her petitions and prayers.
verses.where: Paul tells Timothy how the church is to honor widows, and that families must care for their own first. The widow who is truly alone, he says, puts her hope in God and keeps praying night and day. The church is to stand behind her, not leave her to that hope by herself.

verses.text: Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.
verses.where: James defines pure religion in two parts: care for orphans and widows in their distress, and keeping oneself unstained by the world. The care is the first part, not an extra. A church's faith is measured in part by whether the bereaved among them are visited after the funeral is over.

verses.text: A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord.
verses.where: Paul says a marriage binds as long as both live, and that a widow is free to marry again, as long as it is in the Lord. He adds his own judgment that she may be happier staying as she is. Scripture leaves both roads open, and neither is a betrayal of the one who died.

misread.taken: Jesus' words that in the resurrection people will neither marry nor be given in marriage are sometimes read, or heard by the grieving, as meaning that the marriage did not really matter, that husbands and wives will not know each other, or that the dead become angels.
misread.says: Jesus is answering Sadducees, who denied the resurrection and used a woman married seven times as a puzzle to mock it. He says marriage as we know it belongs to this age, and that the raised will be like the angels in that one way. He does not say that love is lost, that people will not know one another, or that they turn into angels. His point is that God is the God of the living and the dead in him are not lost. Christians hold different hopes about how the love of this life is fulfilled, and it is wise not to claim more than the text says. Nor is the verse any judgment on someone who has married again.
misread.text: In the resurrection, people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven.

whole: If your grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust, a friend, a pastor or a grief counselor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. To lose a husband or wife is to lose the person your days were built around. Scripture calls marriage one flesh, and widows and widowers often describe the loss in the body: the empty side of the bed, the second coffee cup, the habit of turning to say something to someone who is not there. There are new tasks no one taught you, decisions you used to make together, and a social world that often quietly rearranges itself around couples. Some lose a spouse after a long illness, worn out by care; some lose one without warning; some lose one in middle age with children still at home.

The Bible gives the bereaved husband or wife particular attention. Abraham wept for Sarah and then went to buy her a grave. Naomi buried her husband and asked to be called bitter. Anna lived most of her long life as a widow in the temple. Again and again Israel's law and prophets name the widow among the most exposed people in their world, and God calls himself her defender. Scripture names the widow because in its world she had no protector and no income; the grief of a widower is no smaller. Underneath it all is the Song's claim that love is as strong as death. Death is an enemy, and when it parts a husband and wife it tears something God joined.

The wisdom here is first patience. Grief for a spouse does not run on a schedule, and the second year can be harder than the first. It is wise to make no large decisions you do not have to make in the first months, and to let others help with the practical ones. It is also wise to let people in. In Scripture God's care for widows rarely came out of the sky; it came through people, a daughter-in-law who refused to leave, a relative's field left open for gleaning, a church that kept a list and honored those on it. That is why James counts visiting widows as part of pure religion, and why the church that forgets the bereaved after the funeral has forgotten something Scripture puts near the center. If you are the one left, receiving that care is not weakness.

Many who lose a spouse wonder what becomes of the love. Jesus' answer to the Sadducees does not say it is lost; it says God is the God of the living, and that the dead in him are not gone from him. Paul leaves a widow free to marry again or to remain as she is, and neither choice betrays the one who died. Christians who grieve a husband or wife who belonged to Christ grieve with the hope of the resurrection, and the hope does not make the grief smaller. The God who was a defender of widows in Israel has not changed, and the love that was as strong as death answers in the end to a love that defeated it.
deep.sit: Who has offered help that you have not yet let in, and what is one thing you could let them do this week?

prayer.lead: Psalm 146 lists the people the LORD lifts up, and the widow is among them. Pray it as someone on that list.
prayer.text: He executes justice for the oppressed and gives food to the hungry. The LORD sets the prisoners free, the LORD opens the eyes of the blind, the LORD lifts those who are weighed down, the LORD loves the righteous. The LORD protects foreigners; He sustains the fatherless and the widow, but the ways of the wicked He frustrates.

careLines.text: Abraham's tears were not a lack of faith, and yours are not either.
If your grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a grief counsellor.
If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
